title: Reference Cycles

answers: A Weak link is cheaper to clone than an Rc

writing.exampleCaption: The child points back with `Weak`, so the cycle never forms.
writing.explanation:
Two `Rc` handles pointing at each other never reach a count of zero, so neither is freed. `Weak<T>` is the answer: it does not count towards ownership and must be upgraded before use, which turns a parent pointer into something that can legitimately be gone.

Reference counting releases an allocation only when its strong count reaches zero. If node A owns an `Rc` to B and B owns an `Rc` back to A, each keeps the other alive after all outside handles are dropped. Rust prevents memory unsafety here, but the allocations leak. A graph needs a deliberate ownership direction, not strong links in every direction.

A common tree design lets a parent own children through strong `Rc` handles while each child keeps a `Weak` reference back to its parent. A weak reference does not keep the parent alive. `upgrade()` returns an `Option<Rc<T>>`, because the parent may have been dropped. That absence is a normal state to handle, not an exceptional failure. In the sample, `Rc::downgrade` stores the parent link, and the `Option` from `upgrade()` is checked before reading through it.

Draw two nodes and label the strong links before writing code. Remove all external owners on paper: if every node still has an incoming strong link from within the cycle, cleanup cannot begin. Replace one direction with weak links and repeat the count. For practice, create a parent and child, then drop the parent and verify that upgrading the child's weak parent link returns `None` if the child is still held externally. The lesson is not to avoid shared ownership entirely, but to make the owning direction explicit.

Weak references can also be used for caches that should not keep objects alive. The caller must accept that `upgrade()` may return `None`; a weak link is a question about whether the target still exists, not an ownership guarantee. Draw strong and weak edges with different arrows during review.
writing.feedback: Ownership should flow one way; the back-reference observes without owning.

writing.summary: Rust prevents data races, not leaks — a cycle can still strand memory.
